title: North Carolinians Oust a Longtime Prosecutor Known for Fighting Innocence Claims
author: Jacob Biba
content:
Jim O’Neill, a longtime Republican prosecutor who built a record of seeking
harsh sentences and fighting against reviewing past convictions even when
confronted with strong evidence of innocence or racial bias, lost his
reelection bid last week in North Carolina.

He was vying for a fifth term as district attorney of Forsyth County, home to
Winston-Salem. Democrat Amara Hunter, a former Detroit police officer who
later worked as a prosecutor under O’Neill and then as a public defender,
defeated him by more than 13,000 votes, or nearly nine percentage points.

O’Neill became DA in 2009 through an appointment by then-Governor Bev Perdue,
a Democrat, and then ran unopposed as a Republican the first three times he
faced voters. He narrowly defeated a challenger in 2022 but the blue tsunami
that submerged North Carolina this fall proved too much for him in this
Democratic-leaning county. North Carolina Democrats also flipped control of
the state House and broke Republicans’ supermajority in the Senate last week,
and they ousted other local GOP officials such as the [pro-ICE sheriff of
Alamance County](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-county-sheriff-terry-johnson-
shannon-long/), Terry Johnson.

Daryl Atkinson, a civil rights attorney and executive director of the Second
Chance Federation, a nonprofit law firm focused on the restoration of civil
and human rights of formerly incarcerated people, told _Bolts_ that O’Neill
had long been a barrier to progressive criminal justice reform and was
“notoriously punitive.”

O’Neill is known in particular for fighting efforts in North Carolina to
review past convictions and to identify wrongful convictions or miscarriages
of justice.

North Carolina in 2009 passed the [Racial Justice
Act](https://www.wfae.org/race-equity/2024-07-08/were-black-jurors-struck-
because-of-race-question-looms-over-nc-death-penalty-case), which gave
incarcerated people on death row the opportunity to have their sentences
reduced to life in prison without parole if they could prove race played a
significant role in their conviction or sentencing.

O’Neill denounced the Racial Justice Act as a covert effort to end the death
penalty in North Carolina, and in 2012 he hosted dozens of prosecutors from
across the state to train them on how to fight back against motions filed by
death row prisoners.

Later, when O’Neill unsuccessfully ran for attorney general, losing in the
Republican primary in 2016 and four years later to then-Democratic Attorney
General Josh Stein, he [ran as a strong
believer](https://nsjonline.com/article/2019/12/jim-oneill-looks-to-win-n-c-
attorney-general-race) in the death penalty.

The issue matters a great deal in Forsyth County. The most recent execution in
North Carolina, in 2006, was of a man from Forsyth County, and currently nine
of the 122 people on death row are from here. Five of the nine are Black.

When then-Governor Roy Cooper in 2024 commuted the sentences of [15
people](https://governor.nc.gov/news/press-releases/2024/12/31/governor-
cooper-takes-capital-clemency-actions) on death row to life without the
possibility of parole, three were from Forsyth County, though their
convictions were before O'Neill became DA. Cooper faced attacks from the GOP
over his record on criminal justice this year as he ran for Senate, including
by conservative commentator Sean Hannity, who talked about his friendship with
O'Neill while targeting Cooper [on his show in late
October](https://podcastrex.com/shows/the-sean-hannity-show/every-vote-
counts).

O’Neill has also [ripped into the
work](https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/justice/nathaniel-jones-
chris-paul-exoneration-teens-winston-salem/) of the state’s Innocence Inquiry
Commission, which was set up in 2006 ****in****response to several wrongful
convictions, including that of a Forsyth County man,[Darryl Hunt.
Hunt](https://innocenceproject.org/cases/darryl-hunt/) was convicted in 1984
and spent over two decades in prison before his
[exoneration](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/mar/19/darryl-hunt-
exonerated-self-inflicted-gunshot) in 2004.

O’Neill has called the commission, [now called the Post-Conviction Review
Commission](https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/innocence-commission-
state-budget-new-name/), a waste of taxpayer money.

Most recently, O’Neill fought against the exonerations of two Black men who
were convicted in the death of NBA player Chris Paul’s grandfather when they
were teenagers; _The Assembly_ , a statewide news outlet, __has[reported
extensively](https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/justice/nathaniel-
jones-chris-paul-exoneration-teens-winston-salem/) on the questions
surrounding their conviction, including the lack of physical evidence, claims
that police coerced the teens into false confessions, and a key witness who
recanted her testimony.

“The way I see it, this administration of O'Neill has done nothing but defend
the atrocities of the past, many of which involve race and racism,” said Mark
Rabil, a law professor and director of the Innocence and Justice Clinic at
Wake Forest University, in Winston-Salem.

Other state prosecutors have matched O’Neill’s complaints about post-
conviction review, and the N.C. Conference of District Attorneys [successfully
lobbied lawmakers last
year](https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/wrongful-conviction-motion-
appropriate-relief-law-time-limit/) to impose a seven-year limit on when
defendants can file an appeal on their conviction. “Justice requires
finality,” a general counsel for the organization said at the time.

O’Neill did not respond to a request for comment. In a [statement posted on
social
media](https://www.facebook.com/www.ncdistrictattorney.org/posts/pfbid04se5w4Z5L23e9WJYqkoWKSM6zMCJbLXGHpVDZbc6eGtM5NDcay3UugTCG5vkHUHil),
O’Neill said it had “been the honor of my life to serve as your District
Attorney and to stand up for victims and families in this community.” He also
said he was “committed to a smooth transition.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/482061767_1122827839855224_8601290895450001348_n.jpg)The
county courthouse is in Winston-Salem, North Carolina's fifth most populous
city. (Photo via DA's office/Facebook)

O’Neill has also drawn scrutiny for a practice of threatening defendants with
more severe sentences to secure plea deals.

One teen, Terence Smith, turned down a 10-year offer to plead guilty to
charges that he was involved in a 2000 shooting, which Smith maintained he did
not a part in, despite threats by O’Neill, an assistant DA at the time, to add
many more charges if the teen declined, [_Carolina Public Press_ reported in
2023](https://carolinapublicpress.org/60050/stacked-against-when-prosecutors-
stack-charges-against-a-defendant-it-can-mean-a-lifetime-behind-bars/). Smith
was then convicted and sentenced to more than 60 years in prison, and he
remained incarcerated until 2024, when then-Governor Roy Cooper
[commuted](https://governor.nc.gov/terence-smith-commutation-order/open) his
sentence under the [short-lived](https://boltsmag.org/north-carolina-clemency-
juvenile-sentences/) Juvenile Sentence Review Board.

Rabil, who defended Smith at trial, says Forsyth County prosecutors have
continued overcharging as a way to coerce defendants under O’Neill’s
leadership, which he described as a pattern and central to the DA’s office’s
reputation for securing harsh sentences.

“It just causes people to end up pleading just to get it over with after four
or five years, or just to avoid the risk of being executed,” said Rabil, who
continues to work on cases in the county ****and is hopeful this could change
with new leadership.

Hunter, the incoming DA, did not respond to an interview request for this
story. Her campaign had previously declined interview requests unless supplied
with advance questions, which _Bolts_ declined.

She said elsewhere that she would want to bring some changes to the office,
telling [the _Winston-Salem
Journal_](https://journalnow.com/news/local/government-
politics/article_ccf83e5f-ba14-49a7-bd22-28d158aa3037.html) that she opposed
charging so many teens with crimes and said there were many alternatives to
“throwing them into jail with violent criminals.”

She aimed her toughest criticisms at O’Neill’s leadership style. She called
him a “career politician,” noting his unsuccessful runs for statewide office;
besides his two bids for attorney general, O’Neill also ran for lieutenant
governor in 2024, again losing in the Republican primary.

Rabil hopes that, going forward, the DA’s office can make sure that “the
justice system not only runs smoothly but runs fairly and in a non-
discriminatory fashion.” Atkinson echoed Rabil’s wish, telling _Bolts_ that
prosecutors in Forsyth County should “pursue justice, not just punishment.”

Change is needed, Atkinson added, “so we don't completely debilitate people's
ability to progress with their lives.”
